name: Choice Blindness
description: People frequently fail to notice when the outcome of their own choice is covertly swapped for the option they rejected, and will go on to confidently construct coherent reasons defending a preference they never actually held -- a direct challenge to the reliability of introspective self-report about one's own preferences and reasons.
design_relevance_note: A direct, foundational caution for user research and preference elicitation: surveys, A/B-test debriefs, and 'why did you choose this' interviews all rely on introspective accuracy that this phenomenon shows is frequently unreliable, even for the participant's own genuinely-held choices moments earlier.
prevalence_note: Well known within user-research and behavioral-science-literate design circles as a caution against over-trusting self-report, though the specific term 'choice blindness' is less universally recognized than the general concept it names.

findings.description: On a self-transforming paper survey of moral opinions, a full 69% of participants failed to detect at least one of two covert reversals of their own previously stated attitudes, and often went on to construct coherent, unequivocal arguments defending the reversed position as if it had been their own all along — extending choice blindness from single binary choices to broader self-reported attitudes and survey responses.
findings.effect_size: 69% of participants failed to detect at least one of two attitude reversals
findings.source_title: Lifting the Veil of Morality: Choice Blindness and Attitude Reversals on a Self-Transforming Survey

findings.description: The choice-blindness effect extends beyond visual attractiveness judgments to hedonic taste and smell preferences: in a real supermarket tasting-stand setting, shoppers choosing between jam or tea samples often failed to notice when their chosen sample was covertly swapped for the rejected alternative, and produced flavor/aroma-based justifications for a preference they had not actually expressed.
findings.source_title: Magic at the marketplace: Choice blindness for the taste of jam and the smell of tea

findings.description: When choosing which of two presented faces was more attractive, participants frequently failed to detect when the experimenter covertly swapped the outcome shown back to them for the face they had actually rejected, and went on to offer introspectively-derived reasons for a choice they had not, in fact, made — establishing 'choice blindness' as a dissociation between an actual decision and a person's introspective report of that decision's outcome and cause.
findings.source_title: Failure to Detect Mismatches Between Intention and Outcome in a Simple Decision Task
